newsitem.title: USA: Northwest blames line break on ground shift.
newsitem.headline: Northwest blames line break on ground shift.

text.p: Northwest Pipeline Corp said shifting ground was the main contributing factor to ruptures this past weekend on two sections of its 26-inch diameter natural gas pipeline in western Washington.
"While the key factor for the two failures appears to be land movement, the cause of the ruptures remains under investigation," the company said in a statement.
The line near Everson ruptured on Feb 8, while the rupture on the line near Kalama occurred the following day. No injuries were reported in either incident.
Washington state has been pounded this winter by unusually heavy snow and rain, saturating the ground.

As a precautionary measure, Northwest said it has stopped the flow of natural gas in the 26-inch mainline from Sumas to Washougal, Wash., taking the pipeline out of service for approximately 260 miles.
"The parallel 30-inch pipeline will remain in service," the company said late Wednesday in a statement.
Using two helicopters and ground surveys, Northwest said it will begin today a survey of its pipeline rights-of-way along the Interstate 5 highway corridor in western Washington.
Following completion of the survey, the company will propose a plan of action prior to returning each segment to service.
Northwest said it will also install monitoring devices on the 26-inch mainline at the Kalama and Everson sites so it can better detect pipeline stress as a result of land movement.
Northwest said it is still working with the U.S. Department of Transportation Office of Pipeline Safety and state agencies to hone in on the direct cause.
Following this weekend's explosions, Northwest switched service to a parallel, 30-inch diameter line to avoid curtailing any deliveries to local customers.
Northwest Pipeline runs from the San Juan Basin in northwestern New Mexico to the U.S.-Canadian border at Sumas, Wash.
